messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 65
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Cybersecurity Analyst
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 80

# Clinical Vignette: Mere

Mere is a 65-year-old Māori woman who has worked in cybersecurity for nearly three decades. She is methodical, precise, and has built a career on anticipating threats before they materialize. She knows how systems fail. She knows how to read warning signs. What she cannot reconcile — what sits at the center of everything that has unraveled since — is that she saw none of it coming.

Eighteen months ago, Mere was driving home from a conference on a wet winter evening when a logging truck lost control on a coastal highway and crossed into her lane. The collision was catastrophic. Her car was pushed through a guardrail and came to rest partially over an embankment above the sea. She was conscious throughout — trapped for over an hour, the vehicle shifting intermittently beneath her, the sound of metal groaning against rock, water visible below. She remembers thinking, with extraordinary clarity, that she was going to die there alone. Her husband, Tama, had passed two years earlier. There was no one to call. She simply waited, and the car moved, and she waited again.

She survived with a fractured pelvis, three broken ribs, and a lacerated forearm. Physically, she has largely recovered. In every other sense, she has not.

In the weeks following the accident, Mere returned to her apartment and did not leave it for nearly a month. She told colleagues she was healing. She was, in part. But she was also unable to cross in front of a window without ducking. She could not hear rain against the glass without her chest seizing. She began sleeping on the floor beside her bed because the height of the mattress felt, in some way she cannot fully articulate, dangerous.

She returned to work remotely, and her colleagues noticed little change. Mere is good at performing competence. She spends her days monitoring network traffic, identifying intrusions, writing threat assessments — work that requires sustained vigilance, and vigilance is something she now has in terrible abundance. She is hyperalert at her desk for ten hours at a time, scanning, scanning, unable to stop. At night, the scanning does not stop either. She sleeps in fragments of ninety minutes or less, waking to the sound of the truck that is never there.

The dreams are not always the accident itself. Sometimes she is simply in the car again, on the embankment, and Tama is in the passenger seat, and she knows he is already dead but she cannot tell him, and the car keeps shifting. She wakes from these dreams and lies on the floor in the dark and does not know, for a moment, which loss she is grieving.

Mere has begun avoiding the coastal road entirely, adding forty minutes to any drive she takes — on the rare occasions she drives at all. She has declined two in-person conferences this year. She told herself this was practical. She is beginning to understand it is not. She has also noticed that she feels almost nothing when she speaks to her daughter in Auckland, and this frightens her more than the dreams do. She used to be the one who called. She used to be the one who held things together after Tama died. Now her daughter calls, and Mere answers, and she is somewhere behind her own voice, watching herself perform a conversation.

What she describes most often, and with the most difficulty, is not the fear. It is the sense that the woman who was trapped above the water — who waited, and did not die — is somehow not the same woman who drove onto that highway. She cannot find the seam between them. She knows how breaches happen. She knows how systems are compromised from the inside. She just did not expect it to happen to her.
